TRADITIONAL LEAN

Carousel Hearts

Carousel Hearts is a warm, earnest animated film about the restoration of a family carousel business and the restoration of family connection across generations.

Full analysis below
Film · Theatrical April 17, 2026 Analyzed by Debra Ducane 13 min read

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

Carousel Hearts is not a woke trap. The film carries a +7 TRAD margin and TRADITIONAL LEAN verdict. Female protagonists exist but are characterized by personal agency, family values, and community connection rather than ideological messaging. A same-sex couple appears but is presented matter-of-factly without celebration or narrative weight. The primary story focuses on family restoration, intergenerational love, and the beauty of small-town tradition. Traditional values of family loyalty, hard work, and community service are presented as good. No bait-and-switch into progressive ideology in the second half.

Creative Team
DirectorDean DeBlois
Lead ProducerDreamWorks Animation (Universal Pictures)
ComposerJohn Williams (score), Ariana Grande (songs)
Overall Perspective

Carousel Hearts is a warm, earnest animated film about the restoration of a family carousel business and the restoration of family connection across generations.

The film opens with Lucia, a city-dwelling marketing professional, learning that her grandfather is retiring from his carousel restoration business. Lucia grew up in the city; her grandfather stayed in the small town where the family business began decades ago. They have drifted. The business is foundering. Grandpa Marcus is ready to sell to a developer who will demolish the carousel workshop and turn the site into condos.

Lucia decides to spend the summer helping her grandfather restore the business. What begins as a temporary favor becomes a rediscovery. She learns carousel wood-carving from Marcus. She falls in love with Thomas, another restorer who specializes in carousel mechanics. She reconnects with her childhood best friend Sienna, who never left the small town and has built a life of her own there. And gradually, Lucia realizes that what her grandfather built has genuine worth: not just economic value, but cultural and spiritual value.

Dean DeBlois directs with remarkable restraint. There are no musical numbers that stop the plot to deliver ideology. The songs (by Ariana Grande) serve character moments and emotional beats. The animation style is warm and inviting without being saccharine. The carousel itself becomes a character: a work of art built by human hands, carrying meaning across generations, beautiful in itself and as a symbol of what craftsmanship and family dedication can create.

Zendaya brings surprising depth to Lucia. The character could have been a caricature of the city girl learning to appreciate small-town values. Instead, she is portrayed with genuine ambition and real complexity. Lucia loves her city life. She has worked hard to build a career. Coming home is not a simple homecoming; it is a reckoning with the fact that what she chose to leave behind has worth she did not recognize. Zendaya plays this with nuance, avoiding both the cynicism of someone who looks down on small-town life and the sentimentality of someone discovering it for the first time.

Tom Hanks as Marcus is the film's moral center. He is not portrayed as a wise elder waiting to teach his granddaughter the true meaning of life. He is a businessman facing real financial pressure, making a hard decision to retire and let the business go. His acceptance of this fate is presented with dignity. Lucia's insistence that there is another way is what drives the plot. Hanks plays Marcus with the specificity that has become his trademark: a man dealing with concrete problems (a carousel in need of restoration, bills that need paying, the knowledge that his life's work will be demolished) with pragmatism and grace.

Jack Quaid's Thomas is written as a genuinely skilled craftsman. His love of carousel mechanics is presented as a legitimate passion, not as a quirky trait. When he and Lucia bond over restoration work, it is because they both understand that making something functional and beautiful has meaning. The romantic subplot grows from shared values and shared work, not from arbitrary attraction.

Awkwafina as Sienna is the heart of the film's small-town community. She represents the choice to stay, to build a life locally, to invest in one's hometown. The film never frames this choice as a limitation or a settling. Sienna is portrayed as someone who loves her town and has built meaningful relationships there. Her friendship with Lucia is restored through genuine care, not through nostalgia or sentimentality.

What makes Carousel Hearts distinctly traditional is its celebration of craft, intergenerational transmission of knowledge, and the idea that beautiful things made by human hands have intrinsic worth that transcends their market value. The carousel is not presented as a quaint relic. It is presented as a legitimate work of art. The decision to save it is presented as noble. This is structurally conservative: something old is worth preserving, knowledge from elders is worth learning, and community is worth building and maintaining.

The film includes a same-sex couple among the town's residents. They appear in brief scenes. Their relationship is presented matter-of-factly. They are not the subject of the film, nor are they presented in a way that foregrounds their identity as a narrative statement. They are simply people in the town. This is a form of ideological neutrality: diversity exists without becoming the subject. The film's focus remains on the carousel, the family, and the restoration of connection across generations.

John Williams's orchestral score deserves significant credit. The carousel theme is immediately memorable and communicates warmth, tradition, and joy without becoming saccharine. The score emphasizes family moments and builds emotional resonance for scenes of connection and work. Williams's restrained approach means the music enhances rather than overwhelms.

The third act delivers satisfying emotional beats. Without spoiling the resolution, the film concludes with Lucia making a genuine choice to stay and help her grandfather rather than returning to the city. This choice is presented as growth and maturation, not as settling or as a rejection of her ambitions. The carousel is restored. Lucia and Thomas's relationship deepens with genuine promise. Lucia's connection to her grandfather is healed. These plot points are earned through the film's narrative logic.

What is most striking about Carousel Hearts is what it is not. It is not a film that questions traditional family structures or suggests that inherited knowledge is necessarily limiting. It is not a film that treats small-town values with irony or contempt. It is not a film that uses its diverse cast to make ideological statements. It is simply a warm, well-crafted story about connection, craft, and the discovery that what our elders built might be worth preserving.

For families seeking animated entertainment that respects their values without preaching, Carousel Hearts is a genuine gift.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Adult Viewer Insight

Carousel Hearts operates from a philosophical position that is increasingly rare in contemporary animated films: the belief that some things built by previous generations have genuine worth and that the intergenerational transmission of knowledge and values is meaningful. This is not an anti-progress stance. The film is not Luddite. It simply asserts that progress and tradition are not inherently opposed, and that some traditional values (hard work, craft, family connection, community investment) deserve to survive modernity. This moderate conservatism is embedded in the story's structure rather than stated as argument. It is, paradoxically, quite radical in contemporary Hollywood.

Parental Guidance

Rated G. Carousel Hearts is appropriate for all ages. The film celebrates family, intergenerational connection, hard work, and community service. The romantic subplot is age-appropriate. A same-sex couple appears in background scenes. No violence, no inappropriate language, no sexual content. Highly recommended for family viewing.
